profiles.name: Annie J. Magee
profiles.description:
Annie J. Magee was recorded among the members of the National Woman's Party jailed during the 1917-1919 campaign to picket the Wilson White House for woman suffrage. Doris Stevens's appendix gives her term as five days in January 1919.

Two identifications have been proposed and neither is established. Inez Haynes Irwin's history names a "Katherine Magee" arrested on January 27 and sentenced on January 28, 1919 to five days; whether that is the same woman as Annie J. Magee is not documented. Separately, Annie Josephine Stirlith McGee Jackson (May 4, 1873 - April 26, 1934) has been suggested as the person behind the name. Neither link can be made safely without a court or jail ledger, so no dates of birth, death or custody are recorded here and the two candidates are deliberately not merged into this record.

profiles.name: C. Jacobsen
profiles.description:
C. Jacobsen was identified in contemporary records only by that name. The expansion to "Charles Jacobsen", under which this record was previously filed, is unverified.

He was among the defendants convicted in the Chicago mass prosecution of the Industrial Workers of the World. The trial began on April 1, 1918, verdicts were returned on August 17, and sentences were imposed on August 30, 1918. The consolidated convictions were reviewed in Haywood v. United States, 268 F. 795, decided in 1920.

THE SENTENCE IS IN CONFLICT. The National Civil Liberties Bureau's 1919 roster places C. Jacobsen in a one-year group, while a summary of the court minute book reports that twelve defendants received one year and one day. The original judgment is needed to resolve which applies.

His full name, individual conduct, arrest date, exact counts and judgment, prison, admission and release, actual time served, vital dates and photograph are all unresolved.

profiles.name: Claus Gunderson
profiles.description: Claus Gunderson was a North Dakota man prosecuted in federal court in 1918, during the wave of Espionage Act cases heard by Judge Charles F. Amidon in Fargo. He was convicted for using language described as insulting and abusive toward the Red Cross, its work, and its workers, and Judge Amidon sentenced him to ninety days in the Cass County jail. His case is one of the small-town prosecutions documented in studies of the Espionage and Sedition Acts in North Dakota, where personal feuds and wartime hysteria turned stray remarks into federal crimes.

profiles.name: Emanuel Baltzer
profiles.description: Emanuel Baltzer was the lead defendant among roughly two dozen German-Russian socialist farmers from South Dakota prosecuted under the Espionage Act in 1918. Their offense was signing and circulating a petition to the governor that complained about how draft quotas were apportioned among counties, objected to war debt, and threatened to vote him out of office. Convicted, fined, and sent to the federal penitentiary at Leavenworth, the farmers appealed to the Supreme Court in Baltzer v. United States. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes drafted a forceful dissent defending their right to petition, and rather than allow it to be published the government confessed error, the case was sent back, and the charges were dropped in 1919. The suppressed Holmes dissent, unpublished for decades, is now seen as a milestone on his path to the modern First Amendment.

profiles.name: Ernest Gellert
profiles.description: Ernest Gellert was a Hungarian-American socialist and conscientious objector, the younger brother of the radical artist Hugo Gellert. Drafted in 1917, he refused military service on grounds of conscience and was confined at Fort Hancock on Sandy Hook, New Jersey, where he was made to stand at the edge of his own grave-like pit as punishment. On March 8, 1918, he was found shot dead while under military confinement. The Army ruled the death a suicide committed to protest the treatment of conscientious objectors, though the circumstances have long been questioned. His death became a rallying point for critics of the brutal treatment of objectors in World War I military prisons.

profiles.name: James Divins
profiles.description: James Divins was one of the thirteen soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment hanged at Camp Travis, near San Antonio, at dawn on 11 December 1917, after the first Houston-riot court-martial (the "Nesbit case"). The executions were carried out in secret, within a day of sentencing and without the War Department review that would normally have allowed an appeal. The Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny) erupted on 23 August 1917 after Houston police, enforcing Jim Crow, beat and arrested soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment. About 150 soldiers marched on the city; the night left some twenty people dead. In the largest court-martial in U.S. history, 118 men were tried, 19 executed, and 63 sentenced to life imprisonment. In 2023 the U.S. Army set aside all 110 convictions and honorably discharged the soldiers. (Recorded as Private James Divins)

profiles.name: Joseph Stilson
profiles.description: Joseph Stilson was a Lithuanian-American radical who served as Translator-Secretary of the Lithuanian Socialist Federation and, after the 1919 split, of its Communist successor, becoming the highest-ranking Lithuanian-American on the Communist Party of America's Central Executive Committee. During World War I he was prosecuted under the Espionage Act for an anti-conscription campaign waged through the Lithuanian-language newspaper Kova ("Struggle") and circulars such as "Let Us Not Go to the Army." Convicted in federal court in Pennsylvania, he was sentenced to three years' imprisonment, and the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed his conviction in Stilson v. United States, 250 U.S. 583, on November 10, 1919. He chaired the credentials committee at the founding CPA convention in Chicago in September 1919 and was named "under indictment" in an October 1919 Bureau of Investigation surveillance report of party headquarters. (Lithuanian: Juozas Stilsonas)

profiles.name: Vida Henry
profiles.description: Vida Henry was a nineteen-year veteran of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment and a leader in Company I. Vida Henry took command of the soldiers' uprising during the Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny). On the night of 23 August 1917 — after Houston police enforcing Jim Crow had beaten and arrested men of the regiment — Henry formed a column of about 150 soldiers and led them on a march into the city. As the march broke up outside the San Felipe district, he shook hands with the remaining men, told them he intended to take his own life, and was found dead the next morning. Never captured or tried, he was not among the 118 soldiers court-martialed — of whom 19 were executed and 63 imprisoned for life — whose 110 convictions the U.S. Army set aside in 2023. (Recorded as First Sergeant Vida Henry)

profiles.name: William Breckenridge
profiles.description: William Breckenridge was one of the thirteen soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment hanged at Camp Travis, near San Antonio, at dawn on 11 December 1917, after the first Houston-riot court-martial (the "Nesbit case"). The executions were carried out in secret, within a day of sentencing and without the War Department review that would normally have allowed an appeal. The Houston riot of 1917 (the Camp Logan mutiny) erupted on 23 August 1917 after Houston police, enforcing Jim Crow, beat and arrested soldiers of the all-Black 24th Infantry Regiment. About 150 soldiers marched on the city; the night left some twenty people dead. In the largest court-martial in U.S. history, 118 men were tried, 19 executed, and 63 sentenced to life imprisonment. In 2023 the U.S. Army set aside all 110 convictions and honorably discharged the soldiers. (Recorded as Private William Breckenridge)
